performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: A father remembers the fire in his children’s eyes and sees it again in the stars. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings Rückert’s sonnet with Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic, recorded in Berlin’s Jesus-Christus-Kirche in June 1955.

sections.label: A · Cellos and dark flames
sections.mNote: Cellos climb before the baritone enters

sections.label: B · Harp and D-major light
sections.mNote: Harp arpeggios beneath the children’s imagined words

sections.label: A′ · Fate refuses
sections.mNote: Flute and low strings recall earlier phrases

sections.label: Coda · Harp rising into C minor
sections.mNote: Winds hold the final chord after the voice

cues.title: The cellos climb
cues.text: The cellos begin alone, their melody climbing through an octave across the introduction. Winds and plucked strings gather around them. Fischer-Dieskau takes up the same rising shape for “Nun seh’ ich wohl” — now I see clearly.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 18; Rückert’s opening words, our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425. Recording dates and venue: Naxos 8.111300 rear cover, https://cdn.naxos.com/SharedFiles/pdf/rear/8.111300r.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourteen lines about eyes
cues.text: Rückert writes a sonnet: two groups of four lines, then two of three. Its “dunkle Flammen” — dark flames — are the children’s eyes. The father searches their remembered looks for something he failed to understand while they were alive.
cues.evidence: Rückert, Nun seh’ ich wohl, German text reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text; our translation. Sonnet structure discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

cues.title: A publisher at the hotel door
cues.text: Leipzig, 28 November 1904. Mahler has come to conduct his Third Symphony when the owner of C. F. Kahnt calls on him. He writes to Alma at once of a publisher “eager to acquire my new Lieder and Ballads”. Kahnt prints the cycle the following year.
cues.evidence: Mahler to Alma, written immediately after the Kahnt visit of 28 November 1904, in Letters to His Wife, trans. Anthony Beaumont (Faber, 2004), p. 192, quoted in the Mahler catalogue chronology (which also dates Kahnt’s first editions to August 1905): https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: The children answer
cues.text: D major opens beneath the harp’s sweeping arpeggios. The father imagines what the shining eyes were saying: “Wir möchten nah dir immer bleiben gerne” — we would gladly stay close to you always. Mahler marks the voice warm.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 26–27, rehearsal 3: two-sharp signature, harp arpeggios and voice marked warm. Rückert’s third stanza; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eyes become stars
cues.text: Fate refuses the children’s wish. Earlier phrases return around the baritone, and the poem looks ahead to nights when those eyes will be stars. The flute sings above the darker viola and cello lines.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 28–31, rehearsal 4 onwards. Rückert’s last two stanzas and the varied return are discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Berlin, June 1955
cues.text: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau and Rudolf Kempe record the cycle with the Berlin Philharmonic on 20 and 21 June 1955 in the Jesus-Christus-Kirche. Three years earlier, in London’s Kingsway Hall, Fischer-Dieskau had recorded Mahler’s Wayfarer songs with Wilhelm Furtwängler.
cues.evidence: Naxos 8.111300 rear cover: Kindertotenlieder, Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra, Rudolf Kempe, recorded 20th–21st June 1955 in Jesus-Christus-Kirche, Berlin; Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen, Philharmonia Orchestra, Wilhelm Furtwängler, recorded 24th–25th June 1952 in Kingsway Hall, London: https://cdn.naxos.com/SharedFiles/pdf/rear/8.111300r.pdf

cues.title: The harp climbs away
cues.text: After Fischer-Dieskau’s last words, the harp climbs through a chord that seems to promise another key. It settles into C minor. Flutes, clarinets and bassoon hold the chord as the strings disappear.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 32. Woltjer identifies the A♭ seventh chord and its unexpected resolution to C minor: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The harp opens D major
transitions.how: A ritardando holds back “mit eurem”. At Tempo I, the key signature changes to two sharps and the harp spreads a D-major chord. Plucked cellos and basses sound D below; flute, clarinet and bassoon sustain above. The voice opens out on “Leuchten” — shining — marked warm.

transitions.title: The bright answer darkens
transitions.how: The D-major passage moves through A7 into G minor as the children’s imagined wish meets its refusal. The flute carries the high line; violas sustain below. After the vocal phrase, cellos change from plucking to bowing, and horn and bassoon carry fragments into the next stanza.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 27–28, rehearsal 4; harmonic route in Woltjer, song II, bars 44–60. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

transitions.title: An unexpected C-minor landing
transitions.to: Coda · Harp rising into C minor
transitions.how: The strings shorten and soften their phrases after the voice finishes. Over plucked low strings, the harp climbs through an A♭ seventh chord, which could lead to D♭. It resolves into C minor instead. Flutes, clarinets and bassoon hold the last chord, marked morendo — dying away.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 32; Woltjer, song II, discussion of bar 72 and the final cadence. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler2.html

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song II, printed pp. 18–32: the opening cello melody, D-major harp arpeggios at rehearsal 3 and the final C-minor chord.

timeline.note: The cellos begin alone with a rising phrase; winds and plucked strings join them.
The baritone takes up the cellos’ rising melody, surrounded by flute, clarinet and bassoon phrases.
Harp arpeggios open D major beneath the voice; cellos and basses pluck a low D.
Flute and violas sustain while bassoon and horn recall short phrases from the opening.
The harp rises into C minor; flutes, clarinets and bassoons hold the last chord.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
